**On a day in August 2004 one person sat at one ground station and sent two combat aircraft to attack.** The two X-45As flew in coordination for more than an hour under a single operator, with the call signs Stingray 01 and Stingray 02 [[Two Boeing X-45A unmanned jets continue coordinated flights][ref_coordinated_flights]]. **That ratio, one to two, is the entire argument of the programme reduced to a number**, and it is the number this article is about.
This is the forty-sixth article in the [X-Planes series][related_post_a297_framing], following the [X-1][related_post_a298_bell_x1], the [X-2][related_post_a299_bell_x2], the **This is a full-length article and the record supports the length.** Two airframes flew sixty-four times between May 2002 and July 2005, released a weapon, hit a target, flew in formation, replanned in flight and finally prosecuted a multi-target attack under changing operator priorities [[Parsch, Boeing X-45 and X-46, Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles][ref_parsch_x45]]. **The vehicle is documented and its software is not**, so the article dimensions what the software had to deliver rather than describing it.

**The keystone is not aerodynamic and the literature it comes from is not aeronautical.** The quantity that decides whether an unmanned combat aircraft is worth building is the number of vehicles one operator can supervise, and the relation that governs it was written by people studying robots rather than aeroplanes. **At a ratio of one the aeroplane has saved nothing but the pilot's life.** Everything else the concept promises, in crew cost, in persistence and in the willingness to risk the airframe, arrives only when the ratio exceeds one, and the X-45A is where it first did.

## The Research Question

**The binding unknown was whether autonomy could raise the number of aircraft one person can supervise above one.**

That question needs stating carefully, because it is easy to state it in a way that is either trivially true or unfalsifiable. **A remotely piloted aircraft has a ratio of one by construction**, since an operator who never looks away has a neglect time of zero and

$$NT = 0 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad FO = \frac{0 + IT}{IT} = 1$$

The pilot has moved from the cockpit to a container and is committed to that airframe for the whole sortie, and what has been bought is the pilot's survival, a longer endurance than a human bladder allows, and an airframe nobody has to be persuaded to risk. **Those are real and they are not the argument that was being made.** The argument being made was that unmanned aircraft would be cheaper to operate in numbers, and that argument is arithmetic about people.

**The X-45's own programme documents put it in the language of affordability and effectiveness rather than of ratios**, describing a networked system of high performance unmanned air vehicles to prosecute combat missions affordably [[X-45 Unmanned Combat Air Vehicle, NASA][ref_x45_nasa]]. **Affordability in an operational fleet is dominated by people, not by airframes**, and the ratio is the mechanism by which an unmanned aircraft touches that.

**For the second vehicle the question was different and smaller.** The X-45C was to be an operational prototype rather than a demonstrator, and its unknowns were range, payload, carrier compatibility and cost. **It is treated here as the answer to a design question rather than a research one**, and most of the length goes to the X-45A, which is where the research was.

## Programme Origin

**The programme began as a study of whether an unmanned strike aircraft was possible at all.** In the late 1990s the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency began to examine the idea, and in March 1999 Boeing received a contract to build two X-45A technology demonstrators for ground attack, electronic warfare, surveillance and other operations in high-risk airspace [[Parsch, Boeing X-45 and X-46, Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles][ref_parsch_x45]].

**The first airframe was completed in September 2000 and did not fly for twenty months.** It arrived at Dryden in November 2000, the second in May 2001, and both underwent extensive ground and taxi testing through 2001 and into 2002 [[X-45 Unmanned Combat Air Vehicle, NASA][ref_x45_nasa]]. **A twenty-month gap between a finished airframe and a first flight is a statement about where the risk was**, and it was not in the airframe.

**The first flight was on 22 May 2002**, lasting forty minutes and reaching 195 knots at 7,500 feet [[May 22, 2002, the X-45A made its first flight, Air Force Test Center][ref_first_flight_aftc]]. The second vehicle followed in November [[Second Boeing X-45A completes first flight, Boeing][ref_boeing_second_flight]]. **The sixth flight, in December 2002, was the first on which the aeroplane raised its landing gear** [[X-45 Unmanned Combat Air Vehicle, NASA][ref_x45_nasa]], which is a useful measure of how deliberately the envelope was opened.

**The vehicle belongs to a class rather than standing alone** [[Unmanned combat aerial vehicle][ref_ucav_wikipedia]], and its immediate ancestor in the unmanned reconnaissance line is the [DarkStar][ref_darkstar_wikipedia] that the [previous article][related_post_a341_x44_two_aircraft] used to calibrate a thrust lapse.

**In parallel the Navy was building its own.** Two contracts for carrier-based demonstrators were awarded in June 2000, to Boeing for the X-46 and to Northrop Grumman for the X-47, both of which are articles still ahead in this series, and in April 2003 the Air Force and Navy efforts were combined into a joint programme that became Joint Unmanned Combat Air Systems [[Parsch, Boeing X-45 and X-46, Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles][ref_parsch_x45]]. **The X-45B and the X-46A were both cancelled before any airframe was built**, and the joint programme's vehicles were the X-45C and the X-47B.

**The programme was funded to continue.** Boeing received 767 million dollars in October 2004 for the J-UCAS capability demonstration [[Boeing awarded 767 million dollars for the J-UCAS capability demonstration programme][ref_boeing_jucas_award]], and a full-scale X-45C model was shown at Farnborough that July [[Boeing X-45C full-scale model makes its debut at Farnborough][ref_boeing_x45c_mockup]].

**It ended in January 2006.** J-UCAS was cancelled in favour of separate Air Force and Navy programmes, the Air Force turning toward a new manned long-range bomber. The Navy carried the effort forward as a carrier demonstrator competition, and in August 2007 selected the X-47B, terminating the navalised X-45C [[Parsch, Boeing X-45 and X-46, Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles][ref_parsch_x45]]. **The reasons were institutional and the article says so rather than inferring a technical failure that the record does not show.**

## Sizing From First Principles

**The demonstrated result is a ratio, and a ratio has a relation behind it.**

### The Quantity That Decides Whether the Aeroplane Pays

**Let the fan-out be the number of vehicles one operator can supervise.** The term and the relation come from human-robot interaction, where the problem of one person and many machines was posed and measured before it was posed for aircraft [[Olsen and Wood 2004, Fan-out, measuring human control of multiple robots][ref_fanout_acm]]. **The idea is older than the aircraft application and descends from a literature on teleoperation and process supervision** [[Sheridan, Telerobotics, automation and human supervisory control][book_sheridan]].

Let $NT$ be the neglect time, meaning how long a vehicle can be left alone before it needs attention, and $IT$ the interaction time, meaning how long the operator must spend on it once it does. **An operator cycling around a set of identical vehicles can serve them all if and only if the time spent away from any one of them covers the others.** Serving $N$ vehicles takes $N$ interaction times, and each vehicle can wait for at most its neglect time plus the interaction it then receives, so

$$N \, IT \le NT + IT$$

and the largest $N$ satisfying it is the fan-out,

$$FO = \frac{NT + IT}{IT}$$

**The operator's committed time follows immediately and is the quantity an air force actually buys.**

$$\frac{\text{operator hours}}{\text{vehicle hour}} = \frac{1}{FO} \qquad u = \frac{IT}{NT + IT} = \frac{1}{FO}$$

**The operator's utilisation and the reciprocal of the fan-out are the same number**, which is worth noticing because it says a fully occupied operator is a fan-out of one by definition and no amount of interface work changes that.

**The cost argument the programme was actually making follows from it in one line.** With $C_{a}$ the cost of putting an airframe over the target and $C_{c}$ the crew cost of a manned sortie,

$$C = C_{a} + \frac{C_{c}}{FO}$$

**Only the second term responds to autonomy.** An unmanned aeroplane at a fan-out of one has removed the risk to the crew and none of the crew cost, which is the arithmetic behind the claim that the ratio is the whole argument.

**The relation says something the words do not.** Fan-out is not a property of the operator or of the interface alone. It is a ratio of two times, and **autonomy enters it in exactly one place**, by extending the neglect time. An aeroplane that can be left alone for longer can be one of more.

### Inverting It for the Ratio the X-45A Demonstrated

**One operator and two vehicles fixes the ratio, and the relation then fixes the autonomy.** Setting $FO = 2$,

$$2 = \frac{NT + IT}{IT} \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad NT = IT$$

**The X-45A could be neglected for exactly as long as it took to attend to it.** That is the autonomy the vehicle actually had, expressed as a ratio, and no source publishes it in any form.

**It is a modest number and it was a genuine achievement, and both of those are worth saying.** A vehicle that must be attended to half the time is not autonomous in the sense the word is now used. **But the comparison is not with a modern system, it is with a ratio of one**, which is what every armed unmanned aircraft then in service had and what most still have.

### What a Higher Ratio Demands

**The relation is unforgiving about what a better ratio costs.** Rearranging,

$$\frac{NT}{IT} = FO - 1$$

| fan-out | required $NT/IT$ | improvement over the X-45A |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 1 | the demonstrated point |
| 3 | 2 | 2 times |
| 4 | 3 | 3 times |
| 8 | 7 | 7 times |
| 16 | 15 | 15 times |

**The improvement needed is linear in the fan-out and it is measured against a baseline of one**, so a fleet ratio of eight is not four times harder than the demonstrated two. It is seven times harder. **The autonomy has to carry all of it**, because interaction time is bounded below by how fast a human being can understand a situation and decide.

**That is the argument for autonomy stated as arithmetic rather than as enthusiasm**, and it also says where the effort has to go. Halving interaction time and doubling neglect time are worth the same amount, and the first is an interface problem while the second is an autonomy problem.

### The Switch Cost, Which the Original Relation Omits

**An operator moving between vehicles pays for the move.** Later work adds a switch cost $SC$ to the denominator, since the time spent re-establishing context is time not spent on any vehicle,

$$FO = \frac{NT + IT}{IT + SC}$$

| switch cost | fan-out at $NT = 3\,IT$ |
|---|---|
| 0 | 4.00 |
| 0.25 $IT$ | 3.20 |
| 0.50 $IT$ | 2.67 |
| 1.00 $IT$ | 2.00 |

**A switch cost of half the interaction time removes a third of the fan-out.** At a full interaction time it removes half, taking a system designed for four back to the two the X-45A demonstrated without any change to the vehicle at all. **Interface design is therefore not a detail of this problem, it is one of its two terms**, and the ground station is as much the article under test as the aeroplane.

## The Two Aircraft

**The X-45A and the X-45C are not the same design scaled, although the numbers make them look like it.**

| | X-45A | X-45C |
|---|---|---|
| span | 10.3 m | 14.9 m |
| length | 8.08 m | 11.9 m |
| gross mass | 5,530 kg | 16,600 kg |
| thrust | 28.0 kN | 31.0 kN |
| speed | Mach 0.75 | Mach 0.85 |
| ceiling | 35,000 ft | 40,000 ft |
| mission radius | 497 nm | 1,296 nm |
| internal payload | 680 kg | 2,040 kg |

**The two aircraft carry the same payload fraction and that is the fact the rest of the table follows from.**

$$\frac{m_{\text{payload}}}{m_{\text{gross}}} = \frac{680}{5{,}530} = 0.12297 \qquad \frac{2{,}040}{16{,}600} = 0.12289$$

**They agree to four significant figures, and their ratio is 0.99940.** Nothing in the sources says this was intended and the arithmetic says it happened.

**The mass then scales as very nearly the cube of the span, which looks like geometric similarity and is not.**

$$m \propto b^{\,n} \qquad n = \frac{\ln \left( m_{2} / m_{1} \right)}{\ln \left( b_{2} / b_{1} \right)} = \frac{\ln \left( 16{,}600 / 5{,}530 \right)}{\ln \left( 14.9 / 10.3 \right)} = 2.977$$

**The same exponent computed from the payloads instead of the masses gives 2.976**, which is the same number, and that is the explanation.

$$\frac{\ln \left( 2{,}040 / 680 \right)}{\ln \left( 14.9 / 10.3 \right)} = 2.976 \qquad \frac{m_{\text{payload},2}}{m_{\text{payload},1}} = 3.0000$$

**The payload was tripled exactly, the payload fraction was held, and the gross mass therefore tripled too.** The span then followed from the mass rather than the mass from the span.

**It is not geometry and it is not a coincidence either, which is a correction to what this article said before the relation was written down.** The [X-37][related_post_a334_boeing_x37] measured 1.924 against the Shuttle orbiter and the [X-38][related_post_a335_scaled_composites_x38] measured 3.507 against the X-24A, and in both cases the exponent said something about the design. **Here the X-45C's wing planform was changed to the naval one and the two aircraft are not geometrically similar in any other respect**, so an exponent of three is a fact about a held payload fraction and not about a shape. **A scaling exponent that arrives from the mission rather than from the geometry looks identical in the arithmetic and means something entirely different**, which is the warning this series has recorded before against reading an exponent as a property of the technology.

**What is not similar at all is the performance.**

$$\frac{T}{W} = \frac{T_{\text{SL}}}{m \, g} \qquad \left. \frac{T}{W} \right|_{\text{X-45A}} = \frac{28{,}000}{5{,}530 \times 9.80665} = 0.516 \qquad \left. \frac{T}{W} \right|_{\text{X-45C}} = 0.190$$

**A factor of 2.71.** The X-45C is three times the mass on ten percent more thrust, because it is an operational aeroplane carrying three times the payload two and a half times as far, and the demonstrator was a lightly loaded airframe on a proportionally large engine. **Geometrically similar in mass and nothing like each other in the air.**

### A Suspected Error That Did Not Survive Being Checked

**The X-45C's quoted thrust looks wrong and this article expected to report it as wrong.** The engine is given as a General Electric F404 variant at 7,000 pounds force [[Parsch, Boeing X-45 and X-46, Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles][ref_parsch_x45]] [[X-45C, GlobalSecurity][ref_x45c_globalsecurity]], and the F404 family's dry rating is nearer 11,000 with an augmented rating of 17,700 [[General Electric F404][ref_f404_wikipedia]]. **The X-45A's own engine is a Honeywell F124 of 28 kilonewtons** [[Honeywell and ITEC F124][ref_f124_wikipedia]], which is a non-augmented turbofan of the class used in trainers and light attack aircraft. **Parsch himself warns that his figures may be inaccurate.**

**The test available is whether the low figure can hold the vehicle's own stated ceiling.** At the ceiling the thrust available equals the drag, so

$$T_{\text{avail}}(h, M) = \frac{W}{L/D} \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \frac{L}{D} = \frac{W}{T_{\text{avail}}}$$

with the installed thrust following the corrected mass flow of a fixed engine, which is the standard corrected-parameter machinery of engine performance [[Mattingly, Aircraft engine design][book_mattingly_engine_design]] [[Cumpsty, Jet propulsion][book_cumpsty]],

$$T_{\text{avail}} = T_{\text{SL}} \, \frac{p}{p_{\text{SL}}} \, \frac{\left( 1 + 0.2 M^{2} \right)^{3.5}}{\sqrt{\left( T / T_{\text{SL}} \right) \left( 1 + 0.2 M^{2} \right)}}$$

At 40,000 feet and Mach 0.85 the weight is 162.8 kilonewtons and the three candidate ratings give

| sea-level rating | available at the ceiling | lift to drag ratio it demands |
|---|---|---|
| 7,000 lbf as published | 9,964 N | 16.3 |
| 11,000 lbf, the dry class | 15,658 N | 10.4 |
| 17,700 lbf, augmented | 25,195 N | 6.5 |

**A clean subsonic flying wing of this size reaches sixteen to eighteen** [[Torenbeek, Synthesis of subsonic airplane design][book_torenbeek]] [[Filippone, Advanced aircraft flight performance][book_filippone]] [[Raymer, Aircraft design, a conceptual approach][book_raymer]], **so the published figure is admissible and the suspicion does not survive.** What the check produces instead is better than the error would have been, because **it pins a quantity no source publishes.** The X-45C must have achieved a lift to drag ratio of at least 16.3 to do what its own specification says it does.

**The bound is not an artefact of the exact ceiling.**

| assumed ceiling | assumed Mach | required lift to drag |
|---|---|---|
| 35,000 ft | 0.85 | 12.9 |
| 40,000 ft | 0.80 | 17.1 |
| 40,000 ft | 0.85 | 16.3 |
| 40,000 ft | 0.90 | 15.6 |
| 45,000 ft | 0.85 | 20.8 |

**The 40,000 foot rows are all admissible and the 45,000 foot row is not**, since 20.8 is beyond what a flying wing of this size and thickness reaches. **The thrust figure and the ceiling figure therefore pin each other**, and the pair is self-consistent at exactly the ceiling the sources quote. **Two figures that corroborate is a weaker result than an error would have been and a truer one.**

## Dependent Systems

### The Configuration, and the Question the Previous Article Left Open

**The X-45A is tailless, has six trailing-edge elevons and a yaw thrust vectoring nozzle, and has no drag rudders.** In the absence of vertical surfaces yaw was controlled by thrust vectoring [[Parsch, Boeing X-45 and X-46, Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles][ref_parsch_x45]], and eighteen linear electromechanical actuators drove the six elevons, the two-axis nozzle, the nose wheel steering and the landing gear [[Boeing X-45][ref_x45_wikipedia]]. **The absence of a fin is a signature decision before it is an aerodynamic one** [[Knott, Shaeffer and Tuley, Radar cross section][book_knott]], and the configuration has a documented history far older than the jet age [[Wooldridge, Winged wonders, the story of the flying wings][book_wooldridge]]. **The stability the fin would have supplied is replaced by feedback** [[Etkin and Reid, Dynamics of flight][book_etkin_reid]] [[Nelson, Flight stability and automatic control][book_nelson]] [[Anderson, Fundamentals of aerodynamics][book_anderson]].

**That is precisely the configuration the [previous article in this series][related_post_a341_x44_two_aircraft] derived could not meet an operational crosswind landing requirement.** It found that the required vector angle for a crosswind of fixed speed depends on Mach number alone, that at equal throttle the approach is the easiest case in the envelope, and that the approach binds anyway because the throttle is nearly closed. **And then the X-45A landed sixty-four times.**

**The two results are compatible and the arithmetic says why.** The demand goes as the dynamic pressure times the sideslip a fixed crosswind produces, and the authority goes as the thrust the approach leaves available. **Neither the wing area nor the yaw derivative is published for the X-45A**, so the comparison is made against the F-22 case the previous article computed, in which the airframe terms appear in both and the throttle does not.

**The thrust an approach requires is the one relation in this comparison that does not involve the wing at all.** On a glide slope $\gamma$ at a lift to drag ratio $L/D$,

$$\frac{T}{W} = \frac{1}{L/D} - \sin \gamma \qquad \Pi = \frac{W}{T_{\text{SL}}} \left( \frac{1}{L/D} - \sin \gamma \right)$$

which for the X-45A at a landing lift to drag ratio of nine on three degrees gives $\Pi = 0.114$. **The approach speed and the sideslip a crosswind produces do involve the wing**, through

$$V_{\text{app}} = 1.3 \sqrt{\frac{2 m g}{\rho \, S \, C_{L,\max}}} \qquad S = \frac{b^{2}}{A\!R} \qquad \beta = \arctan \frac{V_{c}}{V_{\text{app}}}$$

and the demand the vectoring must meet is the product of the dynamic pressure and that angle,

$$D \equiv q \, \beta = \tfrac{1}{2} \rho V_{\text{app}}^{2} \arctan \frac{V_{c}}{V_{\text{app}}}$$

**The comparison is then a ratio of ratios, in which the airframe constants of the previous article's case appear in both halves and cancel.**

$$\text{margin} = \frac{\Pi / \Pi_{\text{F-22}}}{D / D_{\text{F-22}}}$$

| | X-45A | F-22, from the previous article |
|---|---|---|
| approach thrust fraction | 11.4 percent | 7.2 percent |
| sideslip in a 15 m/s crosswind | 10.1 deg | 11.0 deg |
| demand index, relative | 1.09 | 1 |
| available thrust, relative | 1.58 | 1 |
| **net margin, relative** | **1.45** | **1** |

**The X-45A is better off by a factor of 1.45 and the reason is the throttle.** It is a light aeroplane on a proportionally large engine, so the thrust that a three degree approach requires is a larger share of what the engine can produce, and the vectoring authority scales with that share.

**The wing area is not published and it does real work, so the conclusion is tested across the plausible range.**

| aspect ratio | wing area | wing loading | approach speed | net margin |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3.0 | 35.4 m² | 156 kg/m² | 121 kn | 1.98 |
| 4.0 | 26.5 m² | 209 kg/m² | 139 kn | 1.71 |
| 5.5 | 19.3 m² | 287 kg/m² | 163 kn | 1.45 |
| 7.0 | 15.2 m² | 365 kg/m² | 184 kn | 1.28 |

**Every row leaves the X-45A better off than the F-22, so the conclusion does not depend on the assumed wing.** The thrust fraction does not move at all across that table, because it follows from the glide slope and the lift to drag ratio rather than from the wing, and only the demand column responds.

**The rest of the reconciliation is the previous article's own caveat and not a new argument.** That article said explicitly that a vehicle landing into wind on a long runway at a test range faces a much weaker requirement than an operational fighter does. **The X-45A is exactly that vehicle**, flying at Edwards with the option of waiting for the wind. **So the earlier conclusion survives, the X-45A is not a counterexample to it, and the margin by which it is not a counterexample has been computed rather than asserted.**

### The Weapons Bay

**An internal bay is a hole in a low observable aeroplane, and opening it is the moment the aeroplane stops being one.** The X-45A carried a bay of 680 kilograms capacity, explicitly to test all phases of weapons handling and deployment [[Parsch, Boeing X-45 and X-46, Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles][ref_parsch_x45]], and the X-45C was to carry 2,040 kilograms, being two GBU-31 Joint Direct Attack Munitions.

**In March 2004 the X-45A released a weapon for the first time, and in April it hit a target with an inert satellite-guided bomb** [[Boeing unmanned combat aircraft makes aviation history][ref_aviation_history]]. **The autonomy claim in that milestone is narrower than it is usually reported.** The release was autonomous in the sense that the aeroplane executed it without a pilot flying the aeroplane, and the decision to attack that target had been made by a person. **The distinction matters and is kept throughout**, because the later milestones moved the line and the record says where.

### The Link, and What It Is For

**A supervised aeroplane needs a link, and the link's properties set the interaction time in the fan-out relation directly.** A high-latency or low-bandwidth link raises the time an operator needs to understand a situation and to act, which lowers the fan-out for a fixed autonomy.

**The coupling is not qualitative and writing it down says exactly what a latency figure would be worth.** A round trip of $\tau$ each way is added to every interaction, so

$$IT = IT_{0} + 2\tau \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad FO = \frac{NT + IT_{0} + 2\tau}{IT_{0} + 2\tau + SC}$$

**Latency appears in the numerator and the denominator and does not cancel**, because it lengthens the interaction without lengthening the neglect. Taking a ten second interaction and a neglect time three times it,

| one-way latency | fan-out | cost |
|---|---|---|
| 0 s | 4.00 | none |
| 0.25 s | 3.86 | 3.6 percent |
| 0.5 s | 3.73 | 6.8 percent |
| 1 s | 3.50 | 12.5 percent |
| 2 s | 3.14 | 21.4 percent |

**A satellite round trip costs a fifth of the fan-out on those assumptions**, and a line-of-sight link costs almost nothing. **That is a design consequence rather than an observation**, and it is the reason a supervised combat aircraft wants its operator within line of sight or its autonomy raised to compensate.

**This is the sharpest coupling in the article and the public record does not quantify it for this aeroplane.** No latency figure, no bandwidth figure and no link budget for the X-45A has been released. **The relation says what such a figure would buy and nothing here can say what it was**, which is recorded rather than filled with an assumption.

### Structure and Affordability

**The X-45A used a composite skin over a foam matrix core** [[X-45 Unmanned Combat Air Vehicle, GlobalSecurity][ref_x45_globalsecurity]]. Affordability was a stated programme objective rather than a consequence, and the argument for an unmanned strike aircraft has always been partly that it can be made cheap enough to lose. **No cost figure for the airframe has been released**, so the objective is recorded and not evaluated.

## The Flight Test Record

**Sixty-four flights over thirty-eight months.**

$$\dot{n} = \frac{64}{38} = 1.68 \ \text{flights per month}$$

**That rate is a statement about what was under test.** The airframe was not the article under test after the first year. The software was, and software blocks are validated on the ground between flights rather than in the air. **A programme that flew more often would have been testing something else.**

The record, as the primary directory gives it [[Parsch, Boeing X-45 and X-46, Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles][ref_parsch_x45]], runs in software blocks rather than in envelope points.

| date | milestone |
|---|---|
| May 2002 | first flight, 40 minutes, 195 kn at 7,500 ft |
| November 2002 | second vehicle flies |
| December 2002 | landing gear raised in flight for the first time |
| February 2003 | Block 1 complete, being taxi, takeoff, landing, navigation and basic communication |
| November 2003 | Block 2 testing begins, including communication with manned aircraft |
| March 2004 | first weapon released |
| April 2004 | target hit with an inert satellite-guided bomb |
| August 2004 | two vehicles in coordinated flight under one operator |
| October 2004 | Block 3 begins, including in-flight mission replanning |
| July 2005 | programme complete after 64 flights |

**The final mission is the one worth quoting in full, because it is where the ratio was actually earned.** It included detecting and avoiding multiple simulated threats, determining which of several possible targets to attack, replanning after the operator changed target priorities, and conducting the attacks with one or two aircraft [[Parsch, Boeing X-45 and X-46, Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles][ref_parsch_x45]].

**Read against the fan-out relation, every clause of that sentence is an attempt to raise neglect time.** Detecting and avoiding threats without asking is neglect time. Choosing among targets is neglect time. **Replanning after the operator changed priorities is the opposite**, being an interaction, and it is the one clause that describes the operator doing something. **The mission was designed so that the operator's contribution was a priority change and not a control input**, which is what supervision means.

**Both airframes survived and both are in museums**, one at the National Museum of the United States Air Force [[Boeing X-45A J-UCAS, National Museum of the United States Air Force][ref_x45a_museum]] and one in the Military Unmanned Aerial Vehicles exhibit at the National Air and Space Museum [[Military Unmanned Aerial Vehicles exhibit, National Air and Space Museum][ref_smithsonian_uav]]. **A test programme that ends with every airframe intact is uncommon in this series.**

## What the Data Changed

**The X-45A settled that the ratio can exceed one, and nothing since has settled how far.**

**The demonstrated fan-out of two is still, twenty years later, close to the operational state of the art for armed aircraft.** The vehicles that followed are flown one to one or better in benign airspace and one to one when anything is happening. **A result that has not been beaten in twenty years is either a hard limit or a neglected opportunity**, and the record does not say which.

**The configuration propagated and the programme did not.** The tailless low observable planform with internal carriage is what the X-47B flew from a carrier and what has appeared repeatedly since [[Northrop Grumman X-47B][ref_x47b_wikipedia]]. **J-UCAS itself was cancelled in January 2006 with both competitors' vehicles flying or nearly so**, in favour of separate service programmes and, for the Air Force, a manned bomber.

**The clearest thing the programme changed is what a demonstrator is expected to demonstrate.** The X-45A's milestones are software blocks and not envelope points, and that is now the normal shape of an unmanned aircraft programme. **The aeroplane was the test rig and the flight control laws were the fixture.**

## Where the Framing Breaks Down

**Four places.**

**The fan-out relation assumes homogeneous vehicles and independent tasks, and combat is neither.** Two aircraft attacking the same target are coupled, so neglecting one is not independent of neglecting the other, and the relation's derivation does not hold. **The demonstrated ratio of two is therefore a measurement and the extrapolation to eight is a relation being used outside its assumptions**, which is stated here rather than in a footnote.

**Interaction time is treated as a property of the system and it is a property of a person on a day.** The relation has no term for fatigue, for training, or for the difference between a test operator who helped write the software and a squadron operator who did not. **Every fan-out in this article is therefore an upper bound.**

**The comparison with the F-22 approach borrows a computed case from another article and the two aircraft share no planform.** What transfers is the throttle argument, which depends on the glide slope and the lift to drag ratio, and what does not transfer is anything depending on the wing or the yaw derivative. **Only the part that transfers is used, and the sensitivity table exists to show that the conclusion does not need the rest.**

**Treating the X-45C as an answer rather than a question understates it.** It was a substantial aeroplane that never flew, and an article that gave it equal weight would be a different and more speculative one. **The choice is defensible and it is a choice.**

## The Contemporary Literature

**The survey below maps the field these vehicles sit in and is kept separate from the curated sources that carry the argument.** Every record was harvested from Crossref or from the NASA Technical Reports Server, passed through a subject gate written for this article, and assigned to exactly one cluster.

**The gate for this article carries two anchor families and that was decided before the harvest rather than after it.** The keystone relation comes from human-robot interaction, where the papers carry no aeronautical vocabulary whatever, and an aeronautical gate would have returned none of them. **The previous article learned this twice by rejecting its own foundational sources**, and the lesson is applied here in the only useful direction, which is in advance.

|---|---|

| Autonomy, mission management and onboard decision making | 796 |

### Other aeronautical and autonomy literature

**The residual, reported and not hidden.** On-subject work belonging to no cluster above, including aircraft systems, navigation, sensors, simulation and a long tail of single-topic papers. **A residual of roughly a third is a property of a subject that spans two disciplines**, and no attempt was made to force it down by inventing categories.

### Autonomy, mission management and onboard decision making

**What the X-45A's software blocks were actually delivering.** Mission management architectures, onboard replanning, contingency handling, deliberative and reactive planning, and the long argument about what autonomy means when the word is used as a selling point. **The programme's milestones were all software milestones after the first year**, and this is the field those milestones were drawn from.

### Propulsion, inlet integration and installed performance

**The engine and what the airframe does to it.** Turbofan cycle and installed performance, embedded inlet integration, pressure recovery and specific fuel consumption. **The article uses this literature for one purpose**, being to test whether a published thrust figure can hold a published ceiling.

### Multi-vehicle coordination and cooperative control

**The other half of the fan-out problem, approached from the machine's side.** Cooperative control, task allocation, consensus, distributed decision making, formation flight and swarm coordination. **Autonomy raises the fan-out by raising neglect time**, and this cluster is where the algorithms that do so live.

### Human supervisory control and the span of control

**This is the cluster the article's keystone comes from and it is not an aeronautical literature at all.** It holds human-robot interaction, the fan-out relation and its successors, neglect time and interaction time, operator workload and situation awareness, levels of automation, trust in automation and the out-of-the-loop problem. **A gate written only in the vocabulary of aircraft would have returned none of it**, which is why this article's gate carries a second anchor family declared before the harvest rather than patched in afterwards.

### Suppression of enemy air defences and time-critical targeting

**The mission the vehicle was built for and the one that sets its clock.** Suppression of enemy air defences, emitter location, time-critical targeting, the kill chain, threat evaluation and jamming. **A mobile emitter that shuts down sets a deadline**, and whether the loop closes inside it is the question the mission poses to the autonomy.

### Internal weapons carriage and store separation

**A bay is a hole in a low observable aeroplane and opening it is the moment it stops being one.** Internal carriage, store separation, cavity flow and acoustics, and guided weapon delivery accuracy. **The X-45A released a weapon from an internal bay autonomously in 2004**, which required the separation problem to have been solved on the ground first.

### Flight control law design and handling qualities

**What replaces the pilot's hands.** Control law design, stability augmentation, gain scheduling, adaptive and robust control, and the handling qualities framework that an unmanned aeroplane inherits without inheriting the pilot who defined it. **A handling quality is a statement about a human being**, and this cluster is where the field works out what the term means when there is nobody aboard.

### Verification, validation and the certification of autonomous software

**The reason an autonomous combat aircraft is hard to field rather than hard to fly.** Verification and validation, certification, run-time assurance, safety cases, formal methods and redundancy management. **A demonstrator may fly on a waiver and a fielded aeroplane may not**, and the gap between those two states is where the J-UCAS programme spent its later years.

### What the Shape of the Survey Says

**The autonomy clusters together outweigh the aerodynamic ones and that is the correct shape for this subject.** Autonomy and mission management, multi-vehicle coordination, human supervisory control, and verification of autonomous software hold 1,771 records between them, against 195 for the aerodynamics of the configuration. **An aeroplane whose risk sat in its software has a literature whose mass sits there too.**

**The median publication year is 2016 and 56.4 percent of dated records are from 2015 or later**, which is the most recent distribution this series has measured. The subject did not stop when the programme did. **It moved to a different community**, and the recent weight is in autonomy and cooperative control rather than in combat aircraft.

**Nine hundred and forty-two records predate 2000 and they are not decoration.** Supervisory control was posed as a problem in the 1970s and 1980s for spacecraft teleoperation and nuclear plant operation, long before an aeroplane needed it, and the relation this article rests on is a descendant of that work.

**The datalink cluster is the thinnest at 56 records and the thinness is real rather than an artefact.** Military link performance is largely not published where a bibliographic sweep reaches it. **That is a limit on the survey and not a gap in the field**, and it is the one place where this article's coupling between the link and the fan-out cannot be supported from the literature.

## The Source Base

**The argument rests on six documents and the rest of the reference list is a map of the surrounding literature.**

**One carries the relation.** The fan-out paper defines the term, gives the relation and shows it can be measured empirically [[Olsen and Wood 2004, Fan-out, measuring human control of multiple robots][ref_fanout_acm]]. **Everything done with the keystone comes from that relation and its later extension with a switch cost.**

**One carries the vehicle.** The specialist designation directory gives the programme chronology, the software blocks, the milestone dates, the flight count, the configuration and the specifications of both aircraft [[Parsch, Boeing X-45 and X-46, Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles][ref_parsch_x45]]. **It is a secondary source and it is the best one available**, and it is the only source consulted that states plainly that the X-45A controlled yaw by thrust vectoring in the absence of vertical surfaces.

**Two carry the demonstration.** The contemporary reports of the coordinated flight [[Two Boeing X-45A unmanned jets continue coordinated flights][ref_coordinated_flights]] and of the first weapon release [[Boeing unmanned combat aircraft makes aviation history][ref_aviation_history]] establish the ratio and the date, which is the article's keystone datum.

**Two carry the aeroplane's own numbers.** The government and encyclopaedia entries supply the dimensions, the actuator count and the museum placements [[X-45 Unmanned Combat Air Vehicle, NASA][ref_x45_nasa]] [[Boeing X-45][ref_x45_wikipedia]].

**No primary programme document was located.** No test report, no flight log and no software specification for the X-45A has been found in the open literature. **The analysis below is built so that none of its results depends on one**, resting on published dimensions, a published ratio and a relation from a different field.

**The gate carries two anchor families and the second is narrow on purpose.** It admits the vocabulary of supervising a machine, being supervisory control, fan-out, neglect and interaction time, levels of automation, operator workload and the rest. **It deliberately does not admit bare autonomy, operator, task or workload**, which every discipline that studies work uses.

**Four noise families were added to the shared sweep store, and all four are consequences of the word unmanned.** The civil small-aircraft literature is now far larger than the combat one, so the anchor admits photogrammetry, precision agriculture, flood monitoring and heritage documentation. The aircraft as a telecommunications node is a second family. Unmanned ground, surface and underwater vehicles are a third, sharing autonomy, mission planning and cooperative control completely. Antenna engineering is a fourth, sharing radar cross section. **The cut is by application and never by platform**, because the supervisory-control literature legitimately uses small rotorcraft as testbeds and those results transfer. **Thirty-eight of thirty-nine records mentioning quadrotors survive the patterns and the one that does not is about agricultural spraying.**

**One earlier draft of the antenna pattern would have dropped a paper on radar absorbing material for aircraft radar cross section reduction**, which is exactly on subject, and it was narrowed to microstrip and patch antennas alone. **A pattern is a generalisation and this is the shape of the price.**

## Epistemic State

### Historical Fact

**Boeing received a contract in March 1999 for two X-45A demonstrators.** The first airframe was completed in September 2000 and first flew on 22 May 2002, reaching 195 knots at 7,500 feet in a forty minute flight. The second flew in November 2002.

**The X-45A was tailless with six trailing-edge elevons and a yaw thrust vectoring nozzle, with no vertical surfaces**, and carried an internal weapons bay of 680 kilograms capacity.

**In March 2004 an X-45A released a weapon, in April it hit a target with an inert satellite-guided bomb, and in August 2004 two X-45As flew in coordination under a single operator for more than an hour.**

**The programme ended in July 2005 after 64 flights. J-UCAS was cancelled in January 2006. The X-47B won the Navy competition in August 2007 and the navalised X-45C was terminated.**

**Both X-45A airframes survive in museums.**

### Verified by Independent Derivation

**The fan-out relation returns exactly two when neglect time equals interaction time**, asserted to machine precision.

**The mass exponent of 2.977 was computed from the published spans and masses** and is within one percent of the cube. **The same exponent computed from the payloads is 2.976**, and the two payload fractions agree to four significant figures at 0.12297 and 0.12289.

**The lift to drag ratio the published thrust demands, 16.3, was computed from the standard atmosphere and a corrected-flow engine model**, and the sensitivity across ceiling and Mach number was carried through.

**The crosswind comparison was run across four assumed aspect ratios** and the conclusion holds in every row, with the assertion built into the computation rather than checked by eye.

### Analysis

**The X-45A's demonstrated fan-out of two implies a neglect time equal to its interaction time**, which is the autonomy the vehicle had and is not published anywhere.

**A fleet fan-out of eight requires seven times the neglect-to-interaction ratio the X-45A achieved**, and a switch cost of half the interaction time removes a third of the fan-out.

**The X-45C's published thrust is consistent with its published ceiling and implies a lift to drag ratio of at least 16.3.** The two figures pin each other and would not be consistent at 45,000 feet.

**The X-45A's approach carries 11.4 percent of maximum thrust against 7.2 percent for the F-22 case**, leaving it better off in the crosswind comparison by a factor between 1.28 and 1.98 across the plausible wing.

### Inference

**The twenty-month gap between a completed airframe and a first flight locates the programme's risk in the software.** This is inferred from the chronology and is consistent with the milestone structure.

**The flight rate of 1.68 a month indicates that the aeroplane was a test rig for the flight control laws** rather than the article under test.

**The X-45C is not a scaled X-45A despite a mass exponent of 2.977.** The exponent comes from a held payload fraction and a tripled payload rather than from geometry, which is inferred from the two fractions agreeing and from the changed planform. **This article's draft called the exponent a coincidence of the mission sizing, which was right in direction and wrong to call it a coincidence**, and the correction is carried into the two aircraft section and the conclusion as well as here.

### What the Record Does Not Settle

**Every quantity in the fan-out relation for the X-45A except the ratio itself.** Neglect time and interaction time were not published in seconds, so only their ratio is known.

**The link's latency, bandwidth and budget**, which the article shows to be coupled to the fan-out and cannot evaluate.

**The X-45A's wing area, aspect ratio and yaw derivative**, none of which is published, which is why the crosswind comparison is a sensitivity table.

**What the X-45C would have achieved**, since it never flew.

**Why J-UCAS was cancelled.** The record shows institutional restructuring and a turn toward a manned bomber, and does not show a technical failure.

**Whether a fan-out above two is achievable for armed aircraft at all**, which is the question the programme opened and nothing since has closed.

### On Sources Used With Reservation

**No primary programme document was located and the chronology rests on a secondary directory.** It is careful, it is cited by others, and it warns about its own specification figures. **Every specification in this article inherits that warning.**

**The museum page returns a bot-mitigation status to automated requests** and its existence and title were confirmed by search rather than by retrieval.

### On Information Postdating the Editorial Date

**This article carries an editorial date of 20 November 2025 and is written from knowledge current at the time of writing**, which includes the programme's cancellation, the X-47B selection and two decades of subsequent unmanned aircraft development.

## Out of Scope

**The X-46**, which is the next article in this series and was Boeing's separate naval demonstrator, cancelled before an airframe was built.

**The X-47**, which followed it and won the competition the X-45C lost. Both are treated where the series reaches them, and neither is cited here, because this series cites backward only and an article that cites a sibling not yet published fails the build.

**The suppression of enemy air defences mission in operational detail**, including the emitter timing that would set the loop deadline, which the survey covers and the article does not compute for want of released figures.

**Autonomy verification and certification**, which is the reason an autonomous combat aircraft is hard to field rather than hard to fly, and which deserves its own treatment.

**The cost case**, since no airframe or operating cost figure has been released.

## Conclusion

**The Boeing X-45A is the aeroplane that first made the ratio exceed one.**

**Its keystone is not aerodynamic and its governing relation was written by people studying robots.** Fan-out is the number of vehicles one operator can supervise, it equals one plus the ratio of neglect time to interaction time, and **at a fan-out of one an unmanned aeroplane has saved the pilot's life and nothing else.** In August 2004 one operator flew two X-45As in coordination for more than an hour, which fixes the fan-out at two and therefore fixes the neglect time equal to the interaction time. **That is the autonomy the vehicle actually had, and no source states it in any form.**

**The relation is unforgiving about what more would cost.** A fleet ratio of eight demands seven times that, a switch cost of half the interaction time removes a third of whatever is achieved, and the demonstrated two has not been convincingly beaten for armed aircraft in the twenty years since. **A result that stands that long is either a hard limit or a neglected opportunity and the record does not say which.**

**A third finding came from dividing two numbers the draft had only tabulated.** The X-45A and the X-45C carry the same payload fraction to four significant figures, being 0.12297 and 0.12289, and the payload was tripled exactly. **The near-cubic mass scaling is therefore a consequence of a held payload fraction and not of geometry**, which looks identical in the arithmetic and means something entirely different. **The draft of this article called it a coincidence of mission sizing**, and writing the relation down replaced a vague explanation with a mechanism.

**Two further findings came from checking things this article expected to be wrong.** The X-45C's quoted thrust looks far too low for its engine family, and tested against the vehicle's own stated ceiling it turns out to be admissible and to pin the aeroplane's lift to drag ratio at 16.3 or better, which nobody publishes. **The two figures corroborate rather than conflict, which is a weaker result than an error and a truer one.** And the X-45A flew, sixty-four times, the exact tailless thrust-vectored configuration the [previous article][related_post_a341_x44_two_aircraft] derived could not meet an operational crosswind requirement. **It is not a counterexample.** Its approach carries 11.4 percent of maximum thrust against the 7.2 percent of the case that article computed, leaving it better off by between 1.28 and 1.98 times across every plausible wing, and the rest is the caveat that article already stated, since a demonstrator at a test range may wait for the wind and an operational aeroplane may not.

**What the programme changed is what a demonstrator is now expected to demonstrate.** The X-45A's milestones are software blocks rather than envelope points, its flight rate of 1.68 a month reflects testing that happened mostly on the ground, and its airframe was a fixture for its flight control laws. **The configuration propagated to the aircraft that followed and the programme itself was cancelled with its vehicles flying.** The aeroplane that answered the question is in a museum, and the question it answered is still the one being asked.
